tagline.text: A mangrove and shallow-reef marine sanctuary in northern Siquijor

location.label: Location
location.text: Tulapos barangay coast, Enrique Villanueva, northeastern Siquijor Island

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (per person, entrance, guide and transport)

children.text: Tulapos Marine Sanctuary is a small marine reserve in the town of Enrique Villanueva on northern Siquijor, described as the oldest marine protected area on the island, established in 1986. You can walk in from the beach and tour the mangroves, seagrass beds and shallow reef with a guide, which makes it a good fit for beginners and families.

Tulapos Marine Sanctuary lies on the northeastern coast of Siquijor Island, in Tulapos barangay of the town of Enrique Villanueva. With 6,965 residents in the 2024 census, Enrique Villanueva is the smallest of the island's six towns, covering about 28.6 square kilometers. Tulapos itself has only 834 residents and is a quiet coastal village. The provincial capital, Siquijor town, is about 22 kilometers away along the island's circumferential road. The town was created in April 1924 and is named after Enrique Cayetano Villanueva, a former governor of Negros Oriental; its local name is said to be Talingting. In town you will find Mount Carmel Parish Church and the century-old stilt house known as the Cang-Isok House, both worth a stroll before or after snorkeling. The average temperature is about

and annual rainfall is about 1,047 millimeters. The road links neighboring Larena and Maria easily, and because the sanctuary faces the Bohol Sea on the north coast, early morning is quiet and pleasant.

According to the Snorkeling Report website, this is the island's oldest marine protected area, set up in 1986. Mangroves, seagrass beds and coral reef follow one another in a single line. After you enter from the beach and cross the shallow seagrass, the coral reef begins roughly 200 meters out and slopes gently from about 2 meters deep to about 6 meters. With almost no waves or currents and shallow water, even weak swimmers are reported to manage comfortably in a life vest with a guide.

The big appeal is seeing three landscapes in one outing. Juvenile fish shelter among the mangrove roots; the seagrass holds horned and blue sea stars, mollusks and giant clams; and the outer reef is home to hundreds of reef fish species such as anemonefish, parrotfish, razorfish, triggerfish and butterflyfish. Near the drop-off a school of several hundred barracuda patrols, and green sea turtles are often seen. Turtles do not appear every day, so go with a "lucky if we see one" attitude.

The rules are clear. You pay the entrance fee at the hut at the entrance and are assigned a guide; according to published information, you cannot enter the reserve without one. One guide accompanies every two snorkelers, which helps prevent people from stepping on coral or touching turtles. Unlike many Siquijor spots, this is not a place to wander in freely, take photos and leave.

You enter straight from a sandy beach without a boat, so it is easy on beginners. The entry point is shallow with weak waves, so children can start safely. Life vests and masks can be rented on site, and the guide explains the precautions before you get in.

blocks.title: A nursery of young fish at the mangrove edge

children.text: Juvenile snappers and other young fish hide among the submerged mangrove roots. Mangroves are where fish grow up, so look with your eyes only and do not touch or break the roots.

The seagrass beds, 2–6 feet (about 0.6–1.8 meters) deep, hold horned and blue sea stars, mollusks and dozens of giant clams. You can also see anemonefish living in carpet anemones, a zone children love.

blocks.title: A reef with hundreds of fish species

children.text: About 200 meters from shore the coral reef begins. Branching, tabletop and massive corals remain in fairly good condition, and hundreds of species are said to live there, including parrotfish, razorfish, triggerfish and butterflyfish. The water is shallow, so sunlight reaches the reef and the colors are vivid.

Near the drop-off beyond the reef, at about 6 meters deep, a school of several hundred barracuda has been reported circling slowly. They look intimidating but do not attack people, so keep your distance as your guide instructs.
Green sea turtles are said to visit often, but sightings are not guaranteed. If you do meet one, do not touch or chase it; follow your guide's instructions, keep your distance and watch quietly.
A restaurant called Barakoda stands next to the entrance, a good spot for lunch after snorkeling. Restaurants and accommodation are reported near the entrance.

items.title: Half-day snorkeling plan
items.subtitle: From the morning swim to lunch

children.text: Set off by motorbike or tricycle from your lodging in Siquijor town or Larena. Follow the circumferential road toward Enrique Villanueva and turn toward the sea at the crossing in front of the basketball court.
At the entrance hut, pay the
entrance fee (2023 figure) and the
guide fee (for two people, 2023 figure). Get your life vest and mask and listen to the guide's briefing.
Enter from the sandy beach and tour the seagrass, the mangrove edge and the reef in that order for about
1.5 hours
. Morning currents are weaker and visibility is better.
Come out, rinse off and change. Rest over lunch at the Barakoda restaurant next to the entrance.
On the way back, stop at Salagdoong Beach in Maria or Guiwanon Spring Park in Siquijor town to end the day.
This plan covers the morning only. If you have time, walk the mangrove boardwalk at Guiwanon Spring Park in the afternoon.
Leave Larena port and visit Salagdoong Beach in Maria, known for cliff diving and water slides.
Move on to Enrique Villanueva and snorkel at Tulapos Marine Sanctuary.
Have lunch at Barakoda, then stroll the town church and the coastal road.
Head to Siquijor town and walk the mangrove boardwalk at Guiwanon Spring Park. Admission is about
The most common route is to fly from Manila to Dumaguete (DGT), then take a ferry from Dumaguete port to Siquijor (Larena or Siquijor port). The ferry takes about
40 min–1.5 hours
and fares are reported at about

depending on the vessel class (as of 2026: slower RORO boats ₱130~200, fast craft ₱260~580, possibly higher with fuel surcharges). Boats leave Dumaguete from about 5 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., so check the latest schedule.
You can also go via Cebu: fly from Manila to Cebu, then take a boat or flight from Cebu to Siquijor. Siquijor Airport is small with few scheduled flights, so confirm service in advance.
There is reportedly no regular direct flight from Manila to Siquijor. Schedules change by season, so check before booking.
From Larena port to Enrique Villanueva is a short ride along the circumferential road. Near the port you can rent a motorbike for about
a day, and chartering a tricycle for the day costs about
Your destination is "Tulapos Marine Sanctuary." Turn toward the coast at the crossing in front of the basketball court and you will see the small entrance hut.
The dry season, November to May, has the calmest seas and best visibility for snorkeling on Siquijor. There is less rain, so getting around is easier too.

June to October is the rainy season, with more rainy and windy days. When waves are high or it rains, snorkeling is no longer beginner level, so it is safer to postpone. Mornings usually have lighter wind and better visibility.

items.label: Guide fee
items.note: One guide per two people, 2023 figure (confirm on site)

children.text: Prices are approximate as of

and may vary with local conditions. The entrance and guide fees are 2023 figures, so confirm current rates at the hut. A separate tourism ecological fee (started February 2026) of about ₱50 per person (some sources say ₱100 for foreigners) is paid at the port when you leave Siquijor and is not included above. A June 2026 report says a new SECOTOUR combined ticket for six marine sanctuaries, including Tulapos, costs about ₱499, so ask on site which option is better value.

Next to the Tulapos entrance is the Barakoda restaurant, and other restaurants and lodging are reported nearby. There are not many large resorts, so most visitors stay in Larena or Siquijor town, or on the island's west coast, and make a day trip. The beaches near San Juan on the west side and Siquijor town offer the widest choice of lodging.

Meals are mostly local restaurant fare such as grilled seafood, chicken dishes, and rice with soup. Shopping is limited on the island, so bring snacks and water, and carry plenty of cash. Currency exchange and ATM access on the island can be limited.
The entrance hut was reported in 2023 to be open daily from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Check locally before you visit.
You reportedly cannot enter without a guide. Confirm the official rates at the hut.
Do not step on coral or touch sea stars or turtles. Sunscreen can harm coral, so a long-sleeved rash guard is better.
Bring a waterproof bag, water shoes and snorkel gear. Check whether gear can be rented on site.
Going early in the morning tends to be quieter and calmer.
Bring plenty of cash. Currency exchange and ATM access on the island can be limited.

Fees and rules can change, so check the latest notices. As of June 2026 a new combined ticket for six Siquijor marine sanctuaries (SECOTOUR, about ₱499) exists, and a tourism ecological fee of about ₱50~100 per person is paid separately at the port when leaving the island.

Tulapos and the Tubod Marine Sanctuary in San Juan are on opposite sides of the island, about 22 kilometers (13.6 miles) apart. Combining them in one day takes considerable travel time, so pick one a day and enjoy it unhurried.
Do not enter the water when waves are high, when it is raining, or when currents are strong, and follow your guide's judgment.
Mangroves and seagrass may have sea urchins, so do not walk barefoot.
If you are not a strong swimmer, always wear a life vest and stay close to your guide.
The sun is strong, so bring a rash guard and a hat.
This is a protected area, so leave no trash and do not take coral or shells.
Snorkeling is done at your own risk, so rest if you are not feeling well.
Waves and visibility vary greatly with weather, season and storms. If the sea is bad that day, postpone or switch to another plan.
